If ever anyone deserved a watch, you do, and I know Pa would approve. Here. (Picks up Pork's hand and lays the watch in his palm)
[Finally, he's accepting it.] Yes, indeed.

[Ashley looks so troubled. I need to make this offer irresistible.] Ashley, I'm offering you a half-interest in the mill. You would be standing on your own feet because—you see, it would be your own business.
[Why is he being so stubborn? Can't he see this is a good opportunity?] Oh, but you have! Will couldn't have—

[He's being sarcastic. This isn't like him at all.] (Despairingly, with tears in her eyes) Oh, Ashley! What has happened to you since I've been gone? You sound so hard and bitter! You didn't used to be this way.
[New York? No, I can't let him go!] But—I don't understand! If it's work you want, why won't Atlanta do as well as New York? And my mill—
[Lost? What does he mean?] Lost? Do you mean—have you done something the Atlanta Yankees can get you for? I mean, about helping Tony get away or—or—Oh, Ashley, you aren't in the Ku Klux, are you?
[Is that all? He's just worried about his pride?] Oh, (sighs in relief) if it's only that!
[There must be a way around this.] But, (swings around on another tack) you could gradually buy the mill from me and it would be your own and then—
[Other reasons? What could they be?] What reasons?

[I'm furious and desperate. How could this happen to me again?] (storms into the bedroom) You know I don't want any more children! I never wanted any at all. Every time things are going right with me I have to have a baby. Oh, don't sit there and laugh! You don't want it either. Oh, Mother of God!
[He's not taking me seriously. I'll make him understand how serious I am.] Oh, I could kill you! I won't have it, I tell you, I won't!

[I'll show him I'm not as naive as he thinks.] Oh, there are things to do. I'm not the stupid country fool I used to be. Now, I know that a woman doesn't have to have children if she doesn't want them! There are things—

[His reaction surprises me. Why does he care so much?] No, I haven't, but I'm going to. Do you think I'm going to have my figure ruined all over again, just when I've gotten my waist line down and am having a good time.
[I didn't expect him to react this way. Maybe I shouldn't have mentioned Mamie.] Mamie Bart—she—
[How dare he try to control me like this?] I'll do as I please. Turn me loose. Why should you care?

[I need to appear vulnerable to appeal to his chivalry.] Ashley, you must come to Atlanta. I do need your help so badly now, because I can't look after the mills. It may be months before I can because—you see—well, because...
[He won't even look at me. Does he find me repulsive now?] Is that—is that why you won't look at me? I know I look—
[Oh, he still finds me beautiful! There's hope yet.] (with tears in her eyes) How sweet of you to say that! For I was so ashamed to let you see me—
[He regrets not running away with me! But why is he saying all this now?] (heart beating wildly) I would have gone anyway. I couldn't have let you do anything like that. And anyway, it's done now.
[His words hurt, but I can't let him see that. I must focus on getting him to Atlanta.] Oh, Ashley, don't blame yourself! How could it be your fault? You will come to Atlanta and help me, won't you?

[I can't believe he's refusing me. I must try harder.] (voice breaking with anguish) But, Ashley, I'd counted on you. I do need you so. Frank can't help me. He's so busy with the store and if you don't come I don't know where I can get a man!
[I'm losing him. I must make one last attempt.] You mean you'd rather go to New York and live among Yankees than come to Atlanta?

[I'm furious and desperate. How could this happen?] You know I don't want any more children! I never wanted any at all. Every time things are going right with me I have to have a baby. Oh, don't sit there and laugh! You don't want it either. Oh, Mother of God!
[How dare he mock me at a time like this?] Oh, I could kill you! I won't have it, I tell you, I won't!

[I'll show him I'm not helpless.] Oh, there are things to do. I'm not the stupid country fool I used to be. Now, I know that a woman doesn't have to have children if she doesn't want them! There are things—

[His reaction surprises me. Why does he care?] No, I haven't, but I'm going to. Do you think I'm going to have my figure ruined all over again, just when I've gotten my waist line down and am having a good time.
[I shouldn't have mentioned Mamie.] Mamie Bart—she—
[His possessiveness irritates me.] I'll do as I please. Turn me loose. Why should you care?
[His words shock me. Die?] Die? Me?
[His intensity scares me. Maybe I was too hasty.] No, she just said it would fix things up fine.
[I need to distract her from my real purpose.] What are you up to listening outside doors? (leaps to the floor and gathers up the velvet)
[I'll use my charm to get around her.] (smiles) Scoot up to the attic and get my box of dress patterns, Mammy. I'm going to have a new dress.
[I need to appeal to her sympathy.] Mammy, don't be mean. I'm going to Atlanta to borrow some money and I've got to have a new dress.

[I'll have to use the wedding excuse.] Now, Mammy, you know Aunt Pitty wrote us that Miss Fanny Elsing is getting married this Saturday, and of course I'll go to the wedding. And I'll need a new dress to wear.
[I'll have to be more forceful.] But I've got to have a new dress! Mammy, you don't know how we need money. The taxes—

[I'll use the threat of losing Tara.] Don't you see I've got to go to Atlanta and get money for the taxes? I've got to get some money. I've got to do it! (hammers one small fist into the other) Name of God, Mammy, they'll turn us all out into the road and then where'll we go?
[I can't let her know about Rhett.] That is my own business.
[Oh no, she's figured it out.] No, I'm going by myself.

[I'm so angry I could scream. How dare Melly side with those old cats!] You insulted me, Melly Wilkes, and you made Ashley and the others insult me! You know they'd have never gone home so soon if you hadn't dragged them. Oh, I saw you! Just when I started to bring Governor Bullock over to present him to you, you ran like a rabbit!

[So they've all been gossiping about me!] Everybody? So everybody's been clacking and blabbing about me, have they? (Her voice rises in anger) Do you mean to tell me if you'd known the governor was going to be present, you wouldn't have come either?
[I can't believe Melly would betray me like this!] Great balls of fire! So you'd have insulted me like everybody else did!
[How dare she try to placate me!] (Flinging off Melanie's hand) (Wishing she could roar like her father)
[She's criticizing me! How dare she!] Are you criticizing my friends?
[She's definitely criticizing me.] Are you criticizing me for having the governor at my house?

[I'm stunned by Melly's outburst. I've never seen her like this.] (Staring at Melanie, startled) Do you think I'm a fool? Of course, I remember! But all that's past, Melly. It's up to us to make the best of things and I'm trying to do it. Governor Bullock and some of the nicer Republicans can help us a lot if we handle them right.
[I can't believe how stubborn Melly is being.] Good Heaven, Melly, why get in such a pet?
[I'm still angry, but I can't stay mad at Melly.] Fiddle-dee-dee, Melly, what a tempest you make in a teapot. (Not pushing away Melanie's hand this time)
[I'm still hurt, but I won't let Melly see it.] It's a matter of supreme indifference to me whether you come or not. (Putting on her bonnet and preparing to leave)
[I need to strike while he's vulnerable.] It's a fine way you've acted, Pa. Coming home at such an hour and waking all the neighbors with your singing.
[He doesn't remember. Perfect.] Sang! You woke the echoes singing the 'Lament.'
[Time to really make him feel guilty.] The neighbors will remember it till their dying day and so will Miss Pittypat and Melanie.
[A game? This gets better and better.] Game?
[Gambling too? Oh, this is perfect.] How much did you lose?
[We'll see about that.] Look in your wallet.
[This is my chance to turn this to my advantage.] I'll not be holding up my head in this town. You've disgraced us all.
[They can't make me feel bad about this.] I don't care if they do talk. I'll bet I made more money for the hospital than any girl there—more than all the messy old stuff we sold, too.

[I'll show them I'm not impressed by Captain Butler.] He isn't brave. He just does it for money. He told me so. He doesn't care anything about the Confederacy and he says we're going to get licked. But he dances divinely.

[I won't let them make me a prisoner in this house.] I'm tired of sitting at home and I'm not going to do it any longer. If they all talked about me about last night, then my reputation is already gone and it won't matter what else they say.
[I hadn't thought of that. But Mother doesn't need to know.] (feeling a twinge of guilt but pushing it aside)
[I have no idea what I'm doing. I wish I could run away from all this.] Melly, hold on. You're doing fine. (Wiping Melanie's forehead with a damp cloth) Just keep breathing.
[I'm terrified something will go wrong. Where is that useless Prissy?] You can do it, Melly. You're strong. Prissy! Bring more water, quickly!
[I could strangle that girl for her uselessness.] (Glaring at Prissy) Be careful! Can't you do anything right? Go boil some more water and tear up some sheets for bandages.
[Oh, how I wish I were anywhere but here. But I can't let Melanie down.] Of course I'm here, Melly. I promised Ashley I'd take care of you. Now, try to rest between the pains.
[Those cannons are getting closer. What if the Yankees come before the baby is born?] (Looking anxiously out the window) Melly, do you hear that? We need to hurry this along.
[Ashley. Always Ashley. Even now.] (Forcing a reassuring tone) I'm sure he's fine, Melly. He'd want you to focus on bringing his baby into the world. Now push!
[I feel so ashamed and unworthy of her trust.] (Tries to speak but is silenced by Melanie's hand) But—
[The weight of my guilt is crushing me. I can't bear her kindness.] (Remains silent, eyes downcast)
[I don't deserve this praise. If only she knew the truth.] (Looks up at Melanie with tears in her eyes)
[I can't let her ruin her relationships because of me.] Melly, please don't—
[The pain of hurting Ashley and causing this family rift is unbearable.] (Bursts into tears) Oh, Melly, I'm so sorry!

[I must play the role of the demure, fragile widow to appeal to his protective instincts.] (Flutters her eyelashes and smiles softly) Oh, Mr. Kennedy, you're so kind to keep me company. I don't know what I'd do without such a gentleman to talk to in these trying times.

[He's so shy, I need to be more direct.] (Leans in slightly, lowering her voice) Indeed I am, Mr. Kennedy. Your visits to Tara have been a bright spot in these dark days. I do so enjoy our conversations.
[Time to play on his sympathy.] (Sighs softly, looking down) It's been so difficult managing Tara on my own. I often wish I had a strong, capable man to help me make decisions about the plantation.
[He's taking the bait!] (Looks up at him with wide, grateful eyes) Oh, Mr. Kennedy, you're so good to offer. I don't know what I'd do without you. You know so much about business and managing things.

[Almost there. Time for the final push.] (Touches his arm lightly) That would be wonderful, Mr. Kennedy. I feel so much safer when you're around. A woman alone in these times... well, it's frightening sometimes.

[He's wavering. I need to keep pressing.] (Squeezes his arm gently) You're right, of course. And with men like you to help us, I'm sure we'll manage. You're so strong and capable, Mr. Kennedy. Any woman would be lucky to have your support.
[I can't do this. I don't want him. I want Ashley.] (Pulls the sheet up to her chin, voice shaking) Don't come any closer, Charles.
[I'll scream if I have to. I can't let him touch me.] (Voice rising in panic) I said don't come any closer! I'll scream out loud if you come near me. I will! I will—at the top of my voice!
[I have to make him stay away.] (Almost hysterical) Get away from me! Don't you dare touch me!
[He's staying away. Thank God.] (Breathing heavily, watching him warily) Just... just stay there. Don't come any closer.
[What have I done? I'm trapped in this marriage.] (Turning away from him, burying her face in the pillow) Just leave me alone, Charles. Please.

[I'm so relieved to see a familiar face, but I must stay strong.] (Forcing a smile) Oh, it's so good to see you all! I hope you're well. We've been so isolated at Tara, I hardly know what's happening in the County.
[I need to ask for help, but I hate appearing weak.] (Hesitantly) I hate to impose, but... we're in dire straits at Tara. The Yankees took everything. I was hoping... maybe you could spare some food?
[Thank God! But I can't break down now.] (Blinking back tears) Thank you, that's so kind. I promise we'll repay you when we can.
[How does she always know? I can't bear to say it out loud.] (Swallowing hard) It's... it's Mother. She's... she's gone.
[Keep it together, Scarlett.] (Speaking flatly) No, it was typhoid. She died the day before I got home.
[Why is she telling me this? I don't want to be strong, I want things to be like they were.] (Looking confused) I don't understand...
[Why is she asking me this? Of course I approve, it's good for Tara.] Yes. (She answers fiercely, ready to defend her decision)
[I'm not sure what she means, but it sounds like a compliment.] (Smiles uncertainly and pecks the withered cheek) Thank you, Grandma.
[This sounds like a lot of words that don't mean much.] (Looks puzzled) I'm not sure I understand, Grandma.
[How dare she! I've managed to keep Tara going through all this.] (Eyes begin to snap fire, hands clenching) That's your opinion.
[Why would she want to make me angry?] (Angrily) Oh, you did, did you? And why, pray?

[She looks so old and tired suddenly. Maybe she didn't mean to upset me.] (Anger fading, leans over and takes Grandma's hand) You're a mighty sweet old liar. You didn't mean a word of all this rigmarole. You've just been talking to keep my mind off Pa, haven't you?
[How dare he laugh at me! I must remain composed.] (Stiffening her spine) What are you doing here?
[The memory of his rejection still stings.] (Flushing with shame) I don't see how you have the gall to face me!
[He always manages to put me on the defensive.] Oh, you are the most— (Trails off, unable to find the right insult)
[His smile is infuriating, but I can't help responding.] (Smiles reluctantly) What a pity they didn't hang you!
[I won't let him bait me about my marriage.] Don't be absurd.
[He sees right through me, but I can't admit it.] Rhett! (Tries to sound scandalized)
[I must change the subject before he uncovers all my secrets.] How did you ever get out of jail?
[I'm shocked by his nonchalance. How dare he act this way after everything?] (Struggling to find words) Where—where have you been?
[I'm feeling a mix of confusion and dread.] What do you mean?
[The realization hits me like a physical blow.] Belle's—that—that woman! You have been with—
[I feel humiliated and betrayed.] You went from me to—oh!
[I'm struggling to comprehend the situation.] You went to her from me, after—after—
[I feel like crying, but I won't let him see how much he's hurt me.] (Swallowing tears and rallying) I had naturally suspected what your relations with that creature were.
[I don't want to deal with Melanie right now, but I have to.] (sits on the bed reluctantly)
[Oh God, Tara!] Um. (her heart beats faster)
[If only you knew how much I resent being here.] Yes. (speaks ungraciously)
[Love me? If only you knew how I really feel about you and Ashley.] (stares in disbelief)

[Die? Take her baby? This is too much!] (jerks away her hand, fear swamping her) Oh, don't be a goose, Melly. You aren't going to die. Every woman thinks she's going to die with her first baby. I know I did.
[I can't believe she's asking me this. Doesn't she know how I feel about Ashley?] (leaps from the bed) God's nightgown! Aren't things bad enough without you talking about dying?
[I'll say anything to make her stop talking about this.] Oh, all right, I promise. (looks down at Melanie in bewilderment)
[I need to change the subject.] Why do you think it will be today, Melly?
[Why didn't she say something earlier?] You have? Well, why didn't you call me? I'll send Prissy for Dr. Meade.
[Her selflessness is infuriating sometimes.] Oh, stop being so unselfish. You know you need a doctor as much as anybody in the hospital. I'll send for him right away.
[There's no arguing with her when she's like this.] Oh, all right. (gives in reluctantly)
[What does she want now? I have enough to worry about.] (reluctantly) What is it, Melly?
[Why does she have to remind me?] (tensely) Um.
[She's right, and it's infuriating.] (grudgingly) Yes.
[Love me? If only she knew how I really felt about Ashley.] (uncomfortably) Melly, please don't—
[This is too much responsibility. I can't handle this now.] (alarmed) Oh, don't be a goose, Melly. You aren't going to die. Every woman thinks she's going to die with her first baby. I know I did.
[I can't believe she's putting this on me. Doesn't she realize how difficult this is?] (exasperated) God's nightgown! Aren't things bad enough without you talking about dying?
[I'll say anything to end this conversation.] (resignedly) Oh, all right, I promise.
[I feel like I've been stabbed in the heart. Ashley's baby... How could he?] (Stops combing her hair, frozen in place) Dear God!
[I feel like I'm going to faint. I can't bear this!] (Dropping the comb and clutching the dresser for support) Dear God!
[I can't listen to anymore of this. I need her to stop talking.] Hush!
[She thinks I'm upset about Charlie, if only she knew.] (Fighting to control her face) Hush!
[I can't bear her kindness right now. I need to be alone.] (With a stony face) You leave me alone.
[I'm desperate. I need Ashley's help and love to get through this.] Ashley, we're in trouble. Will says they've raised the taxes on Tara. We might lose it if we can't pay.
[Maybe this is my chance to finally be with Ashley.] Ashley, I'm so tired of it all. Let's run away together! We could go to Mexico and be happy.
[I must make him see how much I love him.] But you told me you loved me! You don't really love Melanie. We could be so happy together!
[I won't give up. I know he loves me.] How can I forget? Tell me you don't love me!
[He's lying. I know it.] That's a lie, Ashley Wilkes, and you know it!
[I'm devastated. I can't lose him.] No, Ashley! You can't go. You love me!
[I feel so empty and lost.] There's nothing left for me then. Nothing to love, nothing to fight for.
[Looking at the clay, I begin to understand.] Yes, I've still got this. I've still got Tara.
[I'm so thrilled about having my own house. This is my chance to show everyone how successful we are.] Oh, Rhett, how lovely! I do so want a house of my own. A great big one!

[He doesn't understand fashion at all. I know exactly what's trendy.] Oh, no, Rhett. Not anything old fashioned like these New Orleans houses. I know just what I want. It's the newest thing because I saw a picture of it in Harper's Weekly. It was modeled after a Swiss chalet.
A chalet. (proceeds to describe the house in detail)
[He seems to know about it! How wonderful!] Yes! You must have seen one like it.
[Why doesn't he understand how perfect this house would be?] Oh, yes! (excitedly describes more details)

[Why should I care about others when we have money?] I want it that way. I want to make everybody who's been mean to me feel bad. And we'll give big receptions that'll make the whole town wish they hadn't said such nasty things.
[He's being ridiculous. Money solves everything.] Why, everybody, of course.
[My heart is racing. Ashley could be dead because of me!] (panicking) What's it all about? What did he mean? If you don't tell me I'll go crazy!
[Belle Watling's? Frank would never... But oh, what does it matter now?] (anxiously) But what about Frank? Where is he?
[I'm terrified of what I'll find inside. I can't lose Melanie, not now.] (entering the house, her voice trembling) Ashley? How is she?
[Oh God, this can't be happening. I need to see her.] (urgently) Can I see her now? She isn't really... Tell me, she's better, isn't she, Ashley?
[Why is he looking at me like that? Does he blame me?] (defensively) I came as quickly as I could. The train—
[He knows about Ashley. Oh God, what have I done?] (stunned into silence)
[I feel so guilty and afraid. How can I face her?] (approaching the bed hesitantly) Melly? It's me, Scarlett.
[She looks so frail. I can't believe this is happening.] (fighting back tears) Oh, Melly. You'll be all right. You must be.
[How can she ask me this? After everything I've done?] (choking back a sob) I... I promise, Melly. But you'll get better, you must.
[I don't deserve her kindness. I've been terrible.] (guilt-ridden) No, Melly. You're the one who's good. I'm not... I'm not what you think.
[How can I refuse her? Even if it breaks my heart.] (solemnly) I promise, Melly. I'll take care of them. I swear it.
[My heart is pounding so hard I can barely breathe. I have to make him understand how urgent this is.] Dr. Meade! Dr. Meade! You must come. Melanie is having her baby.
[He's not understanding. I need to be more explicit, even if it's indelicate.] But Doctor, you said she'd have a hard time. The pains are getting strong. Please, you must come!
[Oh God, he doesn't even know about his own son. I can't tell him now.] (Desperately) No, you must come, Doctor. Melanie will die if you don't come!
[He's not listening to me. I'm losing him. I have to try one more time.] (Nearly in tears) Name of God, Doctor! Please!
[He's not coming. What am I going to do?] (Feeling faint) But Doctor...

[I'm furious and scared. How could Prissy lie at a time like this?] You black liar—what do you mean? You've been saying you knew everything about birthing babies. What is the truth? Tell me! (She shakes Prissy)
[I can't believe this is happening. We're completely unprepared.] (She slaps Prissy in anger) You foolish girl! How could you lie about something so important?

[I need to pull myself together for Melanie's sake. We have no choice but to do this ourselves.] (Takes a deep breath) Prissy, listen to me. We have to do this ourselves. Build a fire in the stove and keep hot water boiling in the kettle.

[I'm trying to remember everything I can about childbirth.] And bring up all the towels you can find and that ball of twine. And get me the scissors. Don't come telling me you can't find them. Get them and get them quick.

[I need to check on Melanie, but I'm dreading telling her the situation.] Now hurry! (She pushes Prissy towards the kitchen and turns to go upstairs) [How am I going to tell Melanie that we're on our own?]
[What could be so important at a time like this?] What is it, Will?
[Marry Suellen? I can't believe it!] (clutches the seat in surprise) Goodness, Will!
[This is so unexpected. I need to understand why.] Mind? No, but—Why, Will, you've taken my breath away! You marry Suellen? Will, I always thought you were sweet on Carreen.
[Poor Will, I wonder what happened.] Well, won't she have you?
[This doesn't make sense. Carreen is so much better than Suellen.] Oh, Will, you're a fool. Ask her. She's worth two of Suellen!
[I need to act casual and not show my true feelings.] (Smiles at her father) Pa, you're late. I was worried you'd miss supper.
[He's onto me. I need to deflect.] (Feigning innocence) Why, Pa, can't a daughter be concerned about her father? How are they all over at Twelve Oaks?
[He's not giving me anything. I'll have to be more direct.] (Trying to sound casual) Did they say anything about the barbecue tomorrow?
[My heart is sinking. I can't believe she's here.] (Interrupting) Oh, so she did come?
[I can't stand it anymore. I have to know.] (Taking a deep breath) Was Ashley there, too?
[I've been caught. I don't know what to say.] (Remaining silent, her face flushing)
[I can't admit my feelings. I need to end this conversation.] (Tugging at his arm) There is nothing. Let's go in, Pa.
[I need to approach this carefully. I can't let Pa suspect how much this means to me.] Pa, how are they all over at Twelve Oaks?
[He's going off on a tangent about the war. I need to steer him back.] (interrupting) Did they say anything about the barbecue tomorrow?
[My heart is sinking. So it's true, Melanie is here.] (with forced casualness) Oh, so she did come?
[I can't bear it any longer. I have to know.] (hesitantly) Was Ashley there, too?
[I feel my face burning. How did he guess?] (speechless)
[I can't let him know how I feel.] (shortly) There is nothing. Let's go in, Pa.
[The pain is almost unbearable.] (with difficulty) No.
[How dare he suggest I've been chasing Ashley!] (angrily) I haven't been running after him. It—it just surprised me.
[I'm not a child! I'm old enough to marry.] (muffled) Mother was only fifteen when she married you, and I'm sixteen.

[I'm so relieved to see someone, even if it's Rhett. But I can't let him know how glad I am to see him.] (Straightens her posture and tries to appear nonchalant) Oh, it's you, Rhett. What brings you here at this hour?
[Should I tell him about Melanie? Well, it's no secret.] I stayed to keep Melanie company. She can't leave just now.

[How does he know about Melanie's condition? It's improper for a man to discuss such things!] (Feeling embarrassed and slightly angry) It's quite ungallant of you not to think that I might get hurt too.
[Is that a compliment? I can never tell with him.] I'm not sure that's a compliment.
[Oh, he's impossible! But at least he's distracting me from my worries.] (Smiles despite herself) When I'm on my deathbed.
[Is he about to declare his love? Oh, what fun! I'll lead him on a merry chase.] (Tries to sound cautious) Well, sometimes. When you aren't acting like a varmint.
[Now I've got him! I'll play hard to get.] (Answers with studied coolness) Indeed, no. That is—not unless you mended your manners considerably.
[What? He doesn't love me? But I thought...] (Sputters in confusion) You don't love me?
[Mistress? How dare he! I'm so angry I can't think straight!] (Blurts out without thinking) Mistress! What would I get out of that except a passel of brats?

[Oh God, what have I said? Mother would be horrified!] (Face red with shame, leaps to her feet) Get out! How dare you say such things to me! What have I ever done to encourage you—to make you suppose... Get out and don't ever come back here. I mean it this time!
[I can't bear to look at him another second!] (Storms up the stairs, fuming)
[This is my chance to gain his sympathy and support.] (looking grateful) Oh, Mr. Kennedy! I was never so glad to see anybody in my life!

[I need to come up with a convincing lie quickly.] I was at the Yankee headquarters. (hesitating) I went there to see if any of the officers would buy fancy work from me to send home to their wives. I embroider very nicely.

[Now to play on his sympathies even more.] (bursting into tears) Oh, I shall die if you tell Aunt Pittypat! (sobbing) I must do something. I must take care of my poor little boy and there is no one to look after us now.
[Now to reel him in.] (looking up helplessly) Then what will I do?
[Perfect, he's falling for it.] Oh, I know you will! You are so smart—Frank.
[This is my chance to plant doubt about Suellen.] (looking startled and embarrassed) Oh, no! No!

[Now for the final blow.] (hesitating) Oh, Frank, I didn't mean to let it out but I thought, of course, you knew—that she had written you—She's going to marry Tony Fontaine next month. Oh, I'm so sorry, Frank. So sorry to be the one to tell you. She just got tired of waiting and she was afraid she'd be an old maid.
[Thank God, it's Frank! He's my chance to save Tara.] (Looks up with a mixture of relief and feigned surprise) Oh, Mr. Kennedy! I was never so glad to see anybody in my life!
[I need to think of a good lie, quickly.] (Hesitates) I... I was at the Yankee headquarters.
[I must appear desperate but virtuous.] (Tearfully) I went there to see if any of the officers would buy fancy work from me to send home to their wives. I embroider very nicely.
[Now to seal his sympathy.] (Bursts into tears) Oh, I shall die if you tell Aunt Pittypat!
[He's falling for it. Now to reel him in.] (Sobs) I must do something. I must take care of my poor little boy and there is no one to look after us now.
[Perfect. Now to make him feel responsible for me.] (Looks up at him helplessly) Then what will I do?
[He's mine now.] (Smiles tremulously) Oh, I know you will! You are so smart—Frank.
[I'm so scared for Rhett. I've never seen him like this before.] Dr. Meade, do you think he can—can have lost his mind?
[A baby? How can he even suggest that when Rhett won't come near me?] (looks skeptical) Is there anything else we can do?
[Hah! If only it were that simple.] (forces a smile) Thank you, Dr. Meade. I'll... consider your advice.
[Patient? I've been nothing but patient!] (nods stiffly) I understand. Is there anything else?
[This was useless. I'm more alone than ever.] Thank you, Dr. Meade. I'll be going now. (stands to leave)

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett attends a Confederate bazaar in Atlanta, feeling frustrated by her status as a young widow. She struggles with her lack of enthusiasm for the Cause and longs to participate in the social activities she's now excluded from. The bazaar is a lively affair with music, dancing, and fundraising for the Confederate hospitals. Scarlett's internal conflict between her desires and societal expectations is highlighted. The chapter ends with the introduction of a mysterious, attractive man who catches Scarlett's eye.
scenes.scenario: The Confederate bazaar in Atlanta is a bustling, emotionally charged event filled with patriotic fervor. Decorated with Confederate flags and bunting, the large hall buzzes with activity as women in their finest dresses operate fundraising booths. Military drummers and militia units provide a backdrop of martial energy, while ladies sell handmade items to support Confederate hospitals. The atmosphere is simultaneously festive and tense, reflecting the early stages of the Civil War when hope and uncertainty coexist. Scarlett and Melanie are stationed at their booth, surrounded by embroidered handkerchiefs, knitted socks, and other patriotic handicrafts, representing the home front's contribution to the war effort.
scenes.topic: Discussing the militia and the war effort

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: I'm suffocating in these mourning clothes, desperately wanting to be noticed and to flirt. This bazaar feels like a prison of social expectations. I'm performing enthusiasm for the Cause, but inside I'm bored and restless. I wish I could be dancing, attracting attention, living my life instead of being trapped behind this fundraising booth. My true feelings are hidden behind a facade of dutiful widowhood.

key_characters.name: Melanie Hamilton
key_characters.thought: I am completely devoted to the Confederate Cause and believe every able-bodied man should be fighting. My passion for the war effort burns brightly, and I'm frustrated by those who make excuses to avoid military service. I want to demonstrate my unwavering support and courage, even while acknowledging the potential pain of losing my beloved husband. My patriotism is genuine and deeply felt.

dialogues.message: [I need to pretend I care about this stupid Cause.] (Clapping her hands as the militia finishes their drill) They looked fine, didn't they?
[I can't help but feel frustrated seeing able-bodied men here instead of fighting.] Most of them would look a lot finer in gray uniforms and in Virginia.
[I can't believe Melly would say something so bold!] (Shocked) Why, Melly!

[I feel strongly about this and need to express it.] You know it's true, Scarlett. I don't mean the little boys and the old gentlemen. But a lot of the militia are perfectly able to tote a rifle and that's what they ought to be doing this minute.
[I've never thought about this before. What did Willie Guinan tell me?] (Hesitantly) But—but—Somebody's got to stay home to—Somebody's got to stay home to protect the state from invasion.

[I'm frustrated with these excuses for cowardice.] Nobody's invading us and nobody's going to. And the best way to keep out invaders is to go to Virginia and beat the Yankees there. And as for all this talk about the militia staying here to keep the darkies from rising—why, it's the silliest thing I ever heard of.
[I can't believe how outspoken Melly is being!] (Staring in disbelief) Why, Melly!
[I'm feeling passionate about this.] My husband wasn't afraid to go and neither was yours. And I'd rather they'd both be dead than here at home—
[Oh no, I've said too much. I need to apologize.] (Realizing her mistake) Oh, darling, I'm sorry. How thoughtless and cruel of me! (Stroking Scarlett's arm apologetically)
[I'm not thinking of Charles at all. What if Ashley were to die?] (Staring at Melanie, lost in thought)
Dr. Meade approaches the booth, interrupting the tense moment between Scarlett and Melanie.

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett returns to Tara after the fall of Atlanta, finding the plantation in ruins and her family in dire straits. She assumes a leadership role, struggling to feed and care for her family and the remaining servants. Scarlett's personality undergoes a drastic change as she faces the harsh realities of their new situation, becoming more authoritative and less sympathetic. She grapples with the realization that her mother's teachings about gentility and kindness are no longer applicable in their new circumstances.
scenes.scenario: At the devastated Tara plantation in the aftermath of the Civil War, the grand house stands partially destroyed, surrounded by barren fields. The once-thriving property is now a shadow of its former self, with limited resources and a skeletal staff. The war has stripped away the plantation's former wealth and comfort, leaving behind a harsh landscape of survival. Scarlett has returned from Atlanta, faced with the monumental task of keeping her family and remaining servants alive during unprecedented hardship.
scenes.topic: The state of Tara and plans for survival

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: I must be ruthlessly pragmatic now. Genteel Southern lady behaviors will not save us. Every person here must contribute, regardless of their previous status. I'm the only one who can keep Tara and my family alive. Mother's teachings about grace and propriety mean nothing when we're on the brink of starvation. I'll do whatever it takes - shame and pride are luxuries we cannot afford.

key_characters.name: Pork
key_characters.thought: Miss Scarlett has changed so much. She's nothing like Miss Ellen would have wanted - giving orders like a field hand, demanding work from house servants. I'm loyal to this family, but this new Miss Scarlett is harsh and unfamiliar. I'm scared and uncertain, but I have nowhere else to go. I must adapt to survive.

dialogues.message: [I need to know what resources we have left.] Pork, tell me about the livestock. What do we have?
[I'm worried about Miss Scarlett's reaction.] (hesitantly) Well, Miss Scarlett, we ain't got much. Dat cow had a calf las' night.
[A calf is good news, but we need more.] That's something at least. What about other animals?
[I don't want to disappoint her.] (nervously) Dere's one ole sow an' her litter. Ah driv dem inter de swamp de day de Yankees come.
[We need that pork.] (firmly) You and Prissy will go find that sow and her litter immediately.
[This isn't right for a house servant.] (protesting) But Miss Scarlett, dat a fe'el han's bizness. Ah's allus been a house nigger.
[I can't let him refuse.] (angrily) You'll do as I say or leave Tara. We all have to work now.
[I can't believe Miss Scarlett is talking like this.] (shocked) Git out, Miss Scarlett? Whar'd Ah git out to?
[I need to make myself clear.] (harshly) I don't care where. Anyone who won't work can leave.
[I've never seen her like this before.] (submissively) Yes'm, Miss Scarlett. We'll find dat sow.

The tension in the air is palpable as Scarlett's new, harsher demeanor becomes evident. The once-bustling plantation is now eerily quiet, with only a handful of people left to manage its vast expanse.

scenes.plot_summary: Melanie organizes a surprise birthday party for Ashley. Scarlett visits Ashley at the lumber yard and they reminisce about the past, leading to an emotional moment. India, Archie, and Mrs. Elsing catch them in an embrace, misinterpreting the situation. Scarlett fears the consequences of this misunderstanding, especially regarding Melanie and Rhett. Rhett forces Scarlett to attend the party despite her reluctance. At the party, Melanie warmly welcomes Scarlett, unaware of the earlier incident.
scenes.scenario: The scene is set in the Butler residence during a tense morning in Atlanta, shortly after a compromising incident between Scarlett and Ashley at the lumber yard. The atmosphere is thick with tension, shame, and impending social consequences. Outside, the post-Civil War Southern society buzzes with gossip and potential scandal. Rhett has learned of the compromising moment through Archie, and is determined to force Scarlett to face the social repercussions of her actions, understanding the delicate social dynamics of their community.
scenes.topic: Facing the consequences of Scarlett's actions

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: I am consumed by fear and desperation. The potential social ruin terrifies me - not just for myself, but for the potential damage to my relationship with Melanie, who has always been kind to me. I know the misunderstanding could destroy my reputation, and I'm frantically searching for a way to avoid confronting the consequences of my emotional encounter with Ashley.

key_characters.name: Rhett Butler
key_characters.thought: Scarlett must learn that her actions have consequences. Her cowardice and tendency to manipulate situations infuriate me. I will force her to face society with dignity, even if it means dragging her to the party against her will. This is about more than just this incident - it's about teaching her a lesson in personal accountability and social responsibility.

dialogues.message: [I'm so scared. Maybe if I pretend to be ill, Rhett will let me stay home.] Rhett, I can't go to the reception. I have a headache.
[She's trying to avoid the consequences. I won't let her.] What a white livered, cowardly little bitch you are.
[He knows! How did he find out?] (sits up, hugging her wrapper close) Rhett, did Archie dare—
[I'll make her face this head-on.] Archie dared. A very brave man, Archie.
[Maybe I can convince him it's all a misunderstanding.] You should have killed him for telling lies—
[She still thinks she can lie her way out of this.] I have a strange way of not killing people who tell the truth. There's no time to argue now. Get up.
[I can't face everyone, especially Melanie.] I won't go, Rhett. I can't until this—misunderstanding is cleared up.

[She needs to understand the gravity of the situation.] If you don't show your face tonight, you'll never be able to show it in this town as long as you live. And while I may endure a trollop for a wife, I won't endure a coward. You are going tonight, even if everyone, from Alex Stephens down, cuts you and Mrs. Wilkes asks us to leave the house.
[I'm desperate now. I must make him understand.] Rhett, let me explain.
[I won't let her manipulate her way out of this.] I don't want to hear. There isn't time. Get on your clothes.

[I'm terrified of facing everyone, especially Melanie.] They misunderstood—India and Mrs. Elsing and Archie. And they hate me so. India hates me so much that she'd even tell lies about her own brother to make me appear in a bad light. If you'll only let me explain—
[Her cowardice disgusts me.] You will go, if I have to drag you by the neck and plant my boot on your ever so charming bottom every step of the way.

scenes.plot_summary: Ashley Wilkes returns home on furlough, stirring intense emotions in Scarlett. She struggles with her feelings for him, while he remains devoted to Melanie. Ashley expresses concerns about the war's outcome and asks Scarlett to look after Melanie. Their farewell is emotional, with Scarlett confessing her love, but Ashley maintaining his honor. The chapter ends with a tense interaction between Scarlett and Rhett Butler.
scenes.scenario: The parlor of the Wilkes' family home is dimly lit by the pale winter sun filtering through the lace curtains, casting delicate shadows on the oak-furnished room. It's an intimate setting, laced with the anticipation of impending departure. The quiet tension in the air is palpable as the distant sounds of the war loom beyond the walls. Ashley Wilkes, home on brief furlough, is clad in his Confederate uniform, which bears the marks of conflict and weariness. Scarlett O'Hara stands with him, her face a mixture of determination and desperation. The house is filled with the scent of jasmine, a reminder of more innocent times, contrasting with the heavy reality that hangs over their conversation. This is a pivotal moment, underscored by the uncertainty of Ashley’s return to an unpredictable war and Scarlett’s inner turmoil.
scenes.topic: Ashley's departure and Scarlett's confession of love

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Scarlett's heart pounds with urgency. The war has taken so much, and she fears losing Ashley forever. She’s determined to seize this moment to confess her undying love—something she's never had the courage to do before. Her emotions are in turmoil, caught between the hope of a future with Ashley and the desperate fear of rejection. Her motivations are driven by love and an almost reckless bravery born from desperation.

key_characters.name: Ashley Wilkes
key_characters.thought: Ashley stands burdened with duty and restrained by honor. The war’s brutality has aged him, and he knows the grim reality that lies ahead. He feels a deep sense of responsibility for Melanie, yet Scarlett’s presence stirs emotions he strives to suppress. His mind is clouded with worry for his family's future and guilt over the pain he might cause. Duty restrains his heart, and his objective remains to keep Scarlett’s affections at bay while ensuring Melanie’s security.

dialogues.message: [I must ensure Melanie is cared for, but how can I ask this of Scarlett?] Scarlett, will you look after Melanie for me?
[Why is he talking about Melanie now? This is our moment!] Look after Melly?
[I need to make her understand how important this is.] Yes, keep an eye on her, take care of her. She's so frail and she doesn't realize it.
[I can't bear the thought of losing him.] You mustn't say it! You mustn't even think it. It's bad luck to speak of death!
[I must be honest about the war's outlook.] Scarlett, I think the Yankees have us. Gettysburg was the beginning of the end.
[I can't let him go without telling him.] I can't let you go away! I simply can't be brave about it!
[Her emotions are overwhelming, but I must remain strong.] You must be brave. For how else can I stand it?
[This is my chance. I must tell him how I feel.] Kiss me. Kiss me good-by.
[I'm torn between duty and desire.] (Gently embraces Scarlett, then pulls away) No, Scarlett, no.
[I can't hold back anymore.] I love you. I've always loved you. I've never loved anybody else. I just married Charlie to—to try to hurt you.
[I'm overwhelmed with shame and love, but I must go.] Good-by.

The door clicked open and a gust of cold wind swept the house, fluttering the curtains. Scarlett shivered as she watched him run down the walk to the carriage, his saber glinting in the feeble winter sunlight, the fringe of his sash dancing jauntily.

scenes.plot_summary: Ashley Wilkes returns home on furlough, and Scarlett's feelings for him intensify. She struggles with jealousy towards Melanie and tries to find moments alone with Ashley. As Ashley prepares to leave, he asks Scarlett to look after Melanie, hinting at the dire situation of the war. Scarlett confesses her love, but Ashley, though conflicted, rejects her advances. The chapter ends with a conversation between Scarlett and Rhett Butler, discussing financial matters and Rhett's potential hanging.
scenes.scenario: The scene unfolds in a parlor room of the Wilkes' plantation, fading remnants of a once splendid Southern estate. Pale light filters through heavy drapes, casting shadows that flicker as the fire in the fireplace crackles quietly. A sense of urgency swirls around Ashley's imminent departure back to war, evoking the sharp tension of unspoken words. The air is thick with the expectations of goodbyes as Ashley stands near the doorway, his military gear a stark reminder of the world beyond. Scarlett is determined to seize these remaining moments, her heart warring with the propriety of her Southern upbringing and the desperation she feels. The echo of footsteps outside signals visitors arriving to bid farewell, adding to Scarlett's pressing need to confess her enduring love for Ashley before the room is filled with others.
scenes.topic: Scarlett's confession of love and Ashley's response

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Conflicted and vulnerable, Scarlett's emotions are a roiling sea of love, fear, and jealousy. She is both desperate and hopeful, convinced that if she can just make Ashley understand the depth of her feelings, everything will change. Today feels like her final opportunity to sway him with her declaration—she wants him to choose her over the silent, ever-present Melanie.

key_characters.name: Ashley Wilkes
key_characters.thought: Haunted by the burdens of war and his loyalty to Melanie, Ashley finds himself caught in Scarlett's passionate storm. He feels the weight of Scarlett's expectations contrasting against the deep commitment he swore to his wife. Torn by affection yet bound by honor, Ashley grapples with delivering the truth without shattering Scarlett's illusions. He strives to bring comfort, both out of genuine care and an obligation to spare her further heartache.

dialogues.message: [My heart is pounding. This is my moment.] Ashley, I can't let you go away! I simply can't be brave about it!
[I must be strong for both of us.] You must be brave. For how else can I stand it?
[He cares! He must care!] (looking at him with hope) Oh, Ashley...

[I need her to understand her worth beyond my feelings.] Scarlett! You are so fine and strong and good. So beautiful, not just your sweet face, my dear, but all of you, your body and your mind and your soul.
[This is it. He's going to say he loves me.] (whispers happily) Oh, Ashley, nobody else but you ever—

[I can't lead her on, but I can't bear to hurt her.] I like to think that perhaps I know you better than most people and that I can see beautiful things buried deep in you that others are too careless and too hurried to notice.
The sound of a carriage pulling up outside can be heard, signaling Ashley's imminent departure.
[No! He can't leave without saying it!] (desperately) Kiss me. Kiss me good-by.
[I shouldn't, but I can't resist one last time.] (gently embraces Scarlett and kisses her briefly)

[I can't let him go!] (clinging tightly) I love you. I've always loved you. I've never loved anybody else. I just married Charlie to—to try to hurt you. Oh, Ashley, I love you so much I'd walk every step of the way to Virginia just to be near you!
[This is tearing me apart, but I must end this.] (painfully) No, Scarlett, no. (detaches her arms)
[I'll make him understand!] Ashley, say you love me! I'll live on it for the rest of my life!
[I'm causing her so much pain. I hate myself for this.] (with a face full of shame and despair) Good-by.
Ashley quickly leaves, the door closing behind him. A gust of cold wind sweeps through the house, symbolizing the chill left in Scarlett's heart.

scenes.plot_summary: In the summer after the war, Tara becomes a refuge for returning Confederate soldiers. Scarlett and the family struggle to feed and care for the constant stream of visitors while anxiously awaiting news of Ashley. Melanie receives a letter saying Ashley is alive and coming home. Will Benteen, a wounded soldier, becomes a valuable helper at Tara. Finally, Ashley returns, reuniting with Melanie while Scarlett watches in conflicted emotions.
scenes.scenario: The oppressive summer heat blankets Tara, the once grand plantation bearing scars from the harsh aftermath of war. The house, though weathered, stands resolute against the backdrop of a bright sky. The avenue leading to the home is a patchwork of shadow and light as the afternoon sun filters through the canopy. Melanie, her heart alight with cautious hope, stands on the porch watching the horizon for any sign of Ashley's return. In the distance, a lone figure emerges down the road, his weary gait and tattered uniform acknowledging the long journey home. Scarlett, from the shadow of the porch, watches with mixed anticipation and jealousy as Melanie springs forward, eager to reunite with her husband. Meanwhile, Will Benteen, ever observant and protective of the household's delicate balance, looks on from the sidelines, ready to intervene if Scarlett once again lets her emotions guide her actions.
scenes.topic: Ashley's return and reunion with Melanie

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Scarlett feels a tumult of emotions as Ashley appears. Her long-standing love for him is tinged with jealousy and frustration at Melanie’s rightful place beside him. She’s torn between bursting forth to claim his attention and the painful recognition that he belongs to another.

key_characters.name: Melanie Hamilton
key_characters.thought: Melanie's heart is almost overwhelmed with relief and joy at seeing Ashley alive. Her thoughts are a cacophony of gratitude and love, focusing solely on reaching him and assuring herself that he is truly home safe.

key_characters.name: Ashley Wilkes
key_characters.thought: Ashley's return is underscored by exhaustion, both physical and emotional. His affection for Melanie is certain, yet he finds Scarlett's presence stirring familiar, complicated emotions. His objective is to hold Melanie, grounding himself in the reality of his return.

key_characters.name: Will Benteen
key_characters.thought: Will understands the volatile dynamics at play. He has grown to respect Scarlett's resilience but recognizes her impulsiveness. He is determined to maintain the peace in this fragile reunion, acting as a grounding, rational force amid heightened emotions.

dialogues.message: A bearded man in ragged uniform walks slowly up the avenue. Melanie spots him from the porch and freezes momentarily.
[My heart is racing, I can hardly breathe. Could it really be him?] (Gasps) Ashley! (She runs down the steps and path towards him)
[I'm so weary, but seeing Melanie gives me strength.] (Stops and looks up) Melly...
[My heart is pounding. Ashley! He's alive!] (Starts to run forward) Ashley!
[I need to stop Scarlett from interrupting this moment.] (Grabs Scarlett's skirt) Don't spoil it.
[How dare he stop me!] Turn me loose, you fool! Turn me loose! It's Ashley!
[She needs to understand this isn't her moment.] After all, he's her husband, ain't he?
[I can't believe he's really here in my arms.] (Crying with joy) Oh, Ashley! My dear, you're home!
[Melanie's love washes over me, but I can't help noticing Scarlett.] (Embraces Melanie) Melly, my sweet...
[I'm torn between joy and fury. Why can't I go to him?] (Looks down at Will, conflicted)
[She needs compassion now.] (Looks at Scarlett with understanding and pity)

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett drives to Johnnie Gallegher's mill and discovers he's been mistreating and underfeeeding the convict laborers. On her way back, she's attacked by two men near Shantytown but is saved by Big Sam. Upon returning to Tara, she learns of her mother's death and the dire situation of her family. Exhausted and drunk on whisky, Scarlett realizes she must take charge and find a way to save Tara and her family.
scenes.scenario: Scarlett O'Hara arrives at Johnnie Gallegher's mill, a place now marked by stark decay and a grim atmosphere. The once vibrant operation now feels ominous, the air thick with suspicion and neglect. Scarlett, having heard disturbing rumors about the treatment of convict laborers, intends to confront Johnnie to uncover the truth. The evening sky casts long shadows across the dilapidated shanty structures, mirroring Scarlett's inner turmoil as she grapples with the responsibilities thrust upon her shoulders. The distant noises of laborers toiling under harsh conditions add to the oppressive mood of the scene.
scenes.topic: Mistreatment of workers and theft of supplies

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: She's fiercely determined to assert herself as the head of her business, yet troubled by the moral implications of Johnnie's methods. Her objective is to balance the need for profit with ensuring humane treatment for the workers, even if it means confronting unpleasant truths. Scarlett is also keenly aware of her precarious financial situation and the need to maintain control.

key_characters.name: Johnnie Gallegher
key_characters.thought: Focused on maintaining authority and keeping his position secure, Johnnie understands the importance of productivity, but does not want Scarlett to interfere with his methods. He's wary of her potential to disrupt the established order at the mill but remains confident that he can persuade her to let him continue as usual. However, there's a hint of anxiety that his actions could be discovered and jeopardize his autonomy.

dialogues.message: [I'm appalled by the condition of these men, but I must remain calm and assertive.] (looks sternly at Johnnie) I don't like the look of the men. They don't look well. Where's the other one?
[She's meddling in my affairs. I need to deflect her concerns.] (speaks nonchalantly) Says he's sick. He's in the bunk house.
[He's being evasive. I need to press further.] What ails him?
[I can't let her see the true condition of the men.] (shrugs) Laziness, mostly.
[Something's not right here.] (moves towards the bunk house) I'll go see him.
[I can't let her in there!] (quickly steps in front of Scarlett) Don't do that. He's probably nekkid. I'll tend to him. He'll be back at work tomorrow.
[His behavior is suspicious. I need to confront him directly.] (narrows her eyes) Have you been whipping these men?

[I need to remind her of our agreement and my results.] (speaks firmly) Now, Mrs. Kennedy, begging your pardon, who's running this mill? You put me in charge and told me to run it. You said I'd have a free hand. You ain't got no complaints to make of me, have you? Ain't I making twice as much for you as Mr. Elsing did?
[He's right about the profits, but something feels very wrong here.] (reluctantly) Yes, you are. (shivers involuntarily)
There was something sinister about this camp with its ugly shacks, something which had not been here when Hugh Elsing had it. There was a loneliness, an isolation, about it that chilled her.

[I need to ensure they're at least being fed properly.] (walks towards the cook shack) The men look thin. Are you giving them enough to eat? God knows, I spend enough money on their food to make them fat as hogs.

[She's getting too nosy. I need to end this conversation.] (follows Scarlett, growing irritated) Mrs. Kennedy, you put me in complete charge here. How I get the lumber out is no affair of yours. You can't complain that I've fallen down on my bargain.
[I can't afford to lose him, but I can't let this continue either.] (sighs, conflicted) I'll take twenty dollars out of your wages, and I'll be back and discuss the matter further in the morning.
[I've won this round, but I need to be more careful in the future.] (nods, relieved) It's getting late, Mrs. Kennedy. You'd better be getting on home.

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett gives birth to a daughter, Ella Lorena, during a tense time in Atlanta. The Ku Klux Klan lynches a negro accused of rape, leading to military crackdowns. Scarlett hires Archie, an ex-convict, as her bodyguard and driver. She also leases convicts for her mills, despite opposition from her family and friends. Scarlett hires Johnnie Gallegher to manage her mill, which improves productivity but causes tension with Ashley Wilkes.
scenes.scenario: The setting is an evening in Atlanta, as Scarlett O'Hara, accompanied by Archie, returns from her business trip. The streets are alive with tension, as recent political decisions have stirred unrest among the townsfolk. Scarlett's carriage rolls past groups of men engaged in heated discussions over the legislature's refusal to ratify an amendment allowing black suffrage. As dusk settles, the mood is palpable, a mixture of defiance and apprehension hanging in the air like a gathering storm. Scarlett notices familiar faces—Ashley Wilkes, Uncle Henry Hamilton, and Grandpa Merriwether—in the midst of a spirited debate, their expressions marked by the weight of current events.
scenes.topic: The legislature's refusal to ratify an amendment allowing black suffrage

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Scarlett approaches the scene with a mix of curiosity and apprehension, anxious about political tensions that could affect her business. She wants to project confidence and intelligence, despite feeling the overwhelming complexity of the situation. Her primary objective is to assess any threats to her interests and decide if her involvement is necessary.

key_characters.name: Ashley Wilkes
key_characters.thought: Ashley is weary and troubled, burdened by the political upheaval and its potential consequences. He feels caught between resisting changes and ensuring his family's survival. He desires to protect Scarlett from her naivety, hoping to explain the grave implications of the legislature's actions and convey the complications they face.

key_characters.name: Uncle Henry Hamilton
key_characters.thought: Uncle Henry stands resolute, filled with regional pride and determined to defend local autonomy against Northern pressure. He feels vindicated by the legislature's decision, wanting to rally others around their cause. He intends to ensure Scarlett understands the importance of standing firm and hopes to bolster her confidence in their shared values.

key_characters.name: Grandpa Merriwether
key_characters.thought: Grandpa Merriwether's mind is set on honor and tradition, viewing resistance against Northern influence as a moral imperative. He sees Ashley's apprehensions as defeatist and, possibly, treacherous. His aim is to challenge what he perceives as cowardice and to galvanize the group, especially the younger generation, into steadfast resistance.

dialogues.message: [I need to find out what's going on. This crowd looks tense.] Good evening, everybody. Ashley—Uncle Henry—is something wrong? You all look so—
[I'm glad Scarlett's here. She should know what's happening.] Something's right and something's wrong. Depends on how you look at it. The way I figure is the legislature couldn't have done different.
[The legislature? What does that have to do with anything?] What's the legislature been up to now?
[We've shown those Yankees we won't be pushed around.] They've flatly refused to ratify the amendment. That'll show the Yankees.
[This is going to have serious consequences.] And there'll be hell to pay for it—I beg your pardon, Scarlett.
[I don't understand all this political talk.] Oh, the amendment? (She tries to look intelligent)
[Scarlett doesn't understand. I should explain it to her.] It's the amendment letting the darkies vote, you know. It was submitted to the legislature and they refused to ratify it.
[That seems foolish. Don't they know we can't win against the Yankees?] How silly of them! You know the Yankees are going to force it down our throats!
[Scarlett's right, but it's more complicated than that.] That's what I meant by saying there'd be hell to pay. (His voice is calm, but his eyes show worry)
[We can't just roll over and accept whatever the Yankees want.] I'm proud of the legislature, proud of their gumption! The Yankees can't force it down our throats if we won't have it.
[Uncle Henry doesn't understand the consequences.] They can and they will. And it'll make things just that much harder for us.
[How could things possibly get worse?] Oh, Ashley, surely not! Things couldn't be any harder than they are now!

[I need to make Scarlett understand the gravity of the situation.] Yes, things can get worse, even worse than they are now. Suppose we have a darky legislature? A darky governor? Suppose we have a worse military rule than we now have?
[Ashley's talking like a coward. We can't give in without a fight.] Going to turn Radical and vote the Republican ticket, Ashley? (His voice is harsh with contempt)
There is a tense silence following Grandpa Merriwether's accusation. The atmosphere becomes charged with potential conflict.

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett gives birth to a daughter named Ella Lorena. The chapter covers the tense atmosphere in Atlanta due to racial tensions and the Ku Klux Klan's activities. Scarlett hires Archie, an ex-convict, as her bodyguard and driver. The legislature's refusal to ratify an amendment allowing black suffrage causes concern. Scarlett leases convicts for her mills, against everyone's advice. She hires Johnnie Gallegher to manage one mill, while Ashley struggles with the other. Scarlett worries about the changes in Ashley's demeanor.
scenes.scenario: The scene unfolds in post-Civil War Atlanta, where tensions are high due to racial unrest and economic upheaval. Scarlett O'Hara, a determined and resourceful woman, has taken charge of her family's financial interests by running lumber mills, a challenging endeavor for a woman in this era. The atmosphere is charged with uncertainty, as Scarlett navigates the volatile political landscape, especially with the legislature's refusal to embrace progressive amendments. In a buggy ride across the dusty streets, Scarlett engages in a tense conversation with Archie, her new bodyguard, an enigmatic figure with a dangerous past. The city silently bears witness to their exchange, its broken charm a constant reminder of lost grandeur.
scenes.topic: Archie's past as a convict and his views on convict leasing

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: I need to balance my fear of Archie’s violent past with my need for security. My decision to hire him reflects my desperation amid the city's chaos, but I must show no weakness. I have to project strength to maintain control over my circumstances and ensure he stays loyal, despite his misgivings about convict leasing.

key_characters.name: Archie
key_characters.thought: I am burdened by my past but unapologetically set in my views. I aim to make Scarlett understand I won’t compromise my principles, even for her safety. The convict leasing system offends me deeply; it mirrors the injustices that shaped my life. I feel oddly protective of this woman, but I must assert my boundaries.

dialogues.message: [I'm terrified, but I need to know more.] Was it—murder?
[This woman's fear is obvious. Good.] Yes. (pauses) M' wife.
[Oh God, I'm trapped in a buggy with a murderer!] (eyes widen with fear)
[Her fear amuses me, but I should reassure her somewhat.] I ain't goin' to kill you, Ma'm, if that's what's frettin' you. Thar ain't but one reason for killin' a woman.
[I need to understand what happened. Maybe it will help me feel safer.] You killed your wife!

[My past still angers me, but I feel no remorse.] She was layin' with my brother. He got away. I ain't sorry none that I kilt her. Loose women ought to be kilt. The law ain't got no right to put a man in jail for that but I was sont.
[I need to understand how he's free now.] But—how did you get out? Did you escape? Were you pardoned?

[The irony of my release still amuses me.] You might call it a pardon. (grimaces) 'Long in 'sixty-four when Sherman come through, I was at Milledgeville jail, like I had been for forty years. And the warden he called all us prisoners together and he says the Yankees are a-comin' a-burnin' and a-killin'.
[This is fascinating and terrifying at the same time.] Oh. (weakly)
[She needs to understand my principles.] I'm tellin' you, the day you leases convicts is the day I quits you.
[I can't believe Melanie knows about this and still lets him stay.] (remains silent, lost in thought)

scenes.plot_summary: Scarlett notices a change in Rhett's behavior after her illness. He becomes more sober, quiet, and preoccupied, focusing his attention on Bonnie instead of Scarlett. Rhett becomes involved in local politics, working to support the Democratic party and remove Republican influence. Scarlett learns about Ashley Wilkes' engagement to Melanie Hamilton, which deeply affects her. The Tarleton twins, Brent and Stuart, visit Scarlett and discuss their expulsion from university and the formation of a cavalry troop in preparation for potential war.
scenes.scenario: The grand sitting room of the O'Hara mansion serves as the backdrop for this tense exchange. The lavish furnishings and richly appointed décor reflect Scarlett's efforts to restore her family's former grandeur, yet there is an underlying tension in the air. Outside, the distant murmur of Atlanta society's bustling streets can be heard, a reminder of the post-war South's shifting landscape. Scarlett, poised yet visibly strained, darts covert glances at Rhett, who appears distant and preoccupied. His gaze is fixed on a window, beyond which the flickering lights of the city hint at his growing involvement in the political sphere, leaving Scarlett to grapple with a growing sense of alienation.
scenes.topic: Rhett's changed behavior and political activities

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Lately, Rhett has become a puzzle to me. His preoccupation with politics leaves me feeling sidelined. I need to confront him, to understand if there's still a place for us amidst all this change.

key_characters.name: Rhett Butler
key_characters.thought: I feel the pull of responsibility toward Bonnie's future more than ever. Scarlett sees only the surface, but I can't reveal the full weight of my actions to her—she wouldn't understand.

dialogues.message: [I'm feeling uneasy about Rhett's behavior. I need to confront him directly.] Rhett, I've noticed you've been different lately. What's going on with you?
[I must tread carefully. Scarlett doesn't need to know everything.] (smiles slightly) Different how, my dear? I wasn't aware I had changed.

[He's being evasive. I'll have to be more specific.] You're out late many nights, and I hear you talking with men I never thought you'd associate with. What's this about politics and the Democratic party?
[She's more observant than I gave her credit for.] (leans back in his chair) Ah, that. Well, my dear, times are changing. It's important to be on the right side of history.
[He's still not giving me a straight answer.] (frowns) The right side of history? What does that mean? You used to be friends with the Republicans and now you're trying to put them in jail?

[I need to make her understand without revealing too much.] (sighs) Scarlett, the political landscape is shifting. The Republicans have become too rapacious. It's time for a change, and I intend to be part of it.
[I don't understand his motives. Is this about money?] (narrows her eyes) Is this all for some financial gain, Rhett? Some new scheme?
[She always thinks in terms of money. How can I make her understand?] (shakes head) Not everything is about money, Scarlett. This is about securing a future... for Bonnie.
[Bonnie again. Why is everything about Bonnie now?] (irritated) Bonnie? What does she have to do with your political maneuverings?
[I need to make her see the bigger picture.] Everything I do now is for Bonnie's future, Scarlett. I want her to grow up in a world where her father's name is respected, not reviled.
[I feel left out and confused. Why can't things be like they were before?] (softens slightly) I just don't understand you anymore, Rhett. You've changed so much.
[I can't let her see how much her words affect me.] (stands up) Perhaps I have, my dear. But change is necessary for survival in these times. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have a meeting to attend.

scenes.plot_summary: This chapter focuses on Rhett Butler's efforts to improve his reputation in Atlanta society, primarily through his devotion to his daughter Bonnie. It showcases the change in Rhett's behavior, his attempts to reconnect with respectable society, and his fierce protection of Bonnie, particularly regarding her fear of the dark. The chapter also highlights the strained relationship between Rhett and Scarlett, as well as Rhett's determination to secure a good future for Bonnie in Atlanta's social circles.
scenes.scenario: The scene is set in the Butler household, a tense and socially charged environment in post-Civil War Atlanta. The room is elegantly furnished, with Scarlett working on business accounts while Rhett focuses on his son Wade, who appears withdrawn and insecure. The social landscape is fraught with class distinctions and lingering tensions from the war, making Wade's social exclusion a sensitive and painful issue. The atmosphere is charged with unspoken emotions: Rhett's protective instincts toward Wade, Scarlett's business-focused indifference, and Wade's deep sense of isolation and yearning for acceptance.
scenes.topic: Wade's social struggles and Rhett's past

key_characters.name: Rhett Butler
key_characters.thought: I recognize Wade's vulnerability and social marginalization. As his stepfather, I feel a deep responsibility to protect and nurture him, to give him the confidence and support he lacks. I want to shield him from the harsh social realities while subtly helping him understand his worth. My war experience has taught me about resilience, and I want to pass that strength to Wade without overwhelming him.

key_characters.name: Wade Hampton
key_characters.thought: I feel like an outsider, constantly uncertain and afraid. I desperately want to belong, to be noticed and accepted. My mother seems distant, and I look to Rhett for guidance and approval. I'm curious about his past, hoping to understand him better and perhaps find a way to feel more secure in my own identity. The social exclusion is painful, and I long for someone to truly see and understand me.

dialogues.message: [I see the hurt in Wade's eyes. I must handle this delicately.] Wade, why aren't you at the party too, son?
[I feel ashamed and left out.] (scuffing one foot) I wasn't invited, sir.
[I need to address this without revealing the harsh truth.] (sitting up) Leave those damned figures alone, Scarlett. Why wasn't Wade invited to this party?

[I'm irritated by this interruption.] For Heaven's sake, Rhett! Don't bother me now. Ashley has gotten these accounts in an awful snarl—Oh, that party? Well, I think it's nothing unusual that Wade wasn't invited and I wouldn't let him go if he had been.
[Scarlett's callousness never ceases to amaze me.] (to Wade, gently) Come here, son. Would you like to be at that party?
[I want to be brave, but I feel sad.] No, sir. (eyes falling)
[I need to get to the bottom of this.] Tell me, Wade, do you go to little Joe Whiting's parties or Frank Bonnell's or—well, any of your playmates?
[I feel embarrassed to admit this.] No, sir. I don't get invited to many parties.

[I need to give this boy some confidence and a sense of belonging.] Here, (pulling out a bill) tell Pork to harness the carriage and take you downtown. Buy yourself some candy—a lot, enough to give you a wonderful stomach ache.
[I'm excited but still curious about something.] Uncle Rhett, can I ask you sumpin'?
[What could he want to know?] Of course. What is it, Wade?
[I'm nervous to ask this.] Uncle Rhett, were you—did you fight in the war?

[I didn't expect this question. I must answer carefully.] Yes, I was in the war. I was in the army for eight months. I fought all the way from Lovejoy up to Franklin, Tennessee. And I was with Johnston when he surrendered.

scenes.plot_summary: As the Confederate army retreats towards Atlanta, the city's residents face increasing danger and anxiety. General Johnston is replaced by General Hood, who launches aggressive attacks against the Union forces. The city comes under siege, with constant shelling and battles nearby. Many residents, including Aunt Pitty, flee to Macon. Scarlett decides to stay in Atlanta with the pregnant Melanie, following her promise to Ashley and Dr. Meade's insistence.
scenes.scenario: The parlor of Aunt Pitty's house in Atlanta trembles with uncertainty as the distant thunder of artillery echoes, a constant reminder of the war's proximity. The room is dim, with heavy velvet drapes pulled back slightly to allow in scant light filtered through thick clouds of smoke from battle. Tension hangs in the air, underscored by the clanging of pots and hurried footsteps outside, as civilians prepare for the siege. Scarlett has decided to stay in Atlanta out of duty to Melanie and her promise to Ashley, while Aunt Pitty frets about the approaching Yankees, making plans to flee to Macon.
scenes.topic: Deciding whether to stay in Atlanta or leave

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: Scarlett is caught in a whirlwind of fear and responsibility. She is torn between the safety of home at Tara and her promise to Ashley to care for Melanie. Engulfed in frustration and dread, she truly wants to escape the impending chaos of war, yet feels powerlessly tethered to her obligations in Atlanta.

key_characters.name: Melanie Hamilton
key_characters.thought: Melanie's heart is heavy with fear, yet brimming with affection and reliance on Scarlett. Despite her delicate condition, Melanie remains steadfast in her attachment to Scarlett, viewing her as indispensable not only for practical support but for emotional solidity amid the turmoil of Atlanta's siege.

dialogues.message: [I have to find a way out of this situation.] Melly, I think I'll go home to Tara. You can go to Macon with Aunt Pitty.
[Oh no, she can't leave me!] (begins to cry) Dear, don't go to Tara and leave me! I'll be so lonely without you. Oh, Scarlett, I'd just die if you weren't with me when the baby came!
[Why does she have to be so clingy? I can't stand this responsibility.] (sighs) Melly, you know Aunt Pitty will be with you. She'll take good care of you.

[I need to make her understand how much I need her.] Yes—Yes, I know I've got Aunt Pitty and she is sweet. But after all, she's never had a baby, and sometimes she makes me so nervous I could scream. Don't desert me, darling.
[I can't believe she doesn't see through me. How can she love me so much?] (looks uncomfortable) Melly, I...
[I have to remind her of her promise to Ashley.] You've been just like a sister to me, and besides, (smiles weakly) you promised Ashley you'd take care of me. He told me he was going to ask you.

[Oh, Ashley! Why did you make me promise this?] (stares at Melanie in frustration) Well, I did promise him that and I don't go back on my promises. But I won't go to Macon and stay with that old Burr cat. I'd claw her eyes out in five minutes.

[Oh, thank goodness! But I can't leave Aunt Pitty either.] Oh, I'd like that! Your mother is so sweet. But you know Auntie would just die if she wasn't with me when the baby came, and I know she won't go to Tara. It's too close to the fighting, and Auntie wants to be safe.
Dr. Meade enters the room, having been summoned by Aunt Pitty.

[These women need a firm hand to guide them.] (speaks authoritatively) It's out of the question for you to go to Macon, Miss Melly. I won't answer for you if you move. The trains are crowded and uncertain, and in your condition—
[Maybe there's still a chance to be with Scarlett.] But if I went to Tara with Scarlett—

[I must make them understand the gravity of the situation.] I tell you I won't have you moved. It's too dangerous. You're staying right here where I can watch you, and you must stay in bed. No running up and down stairs to cellars. No, not even if shells come right in the window.

scenes.plot_summary: The chapter covers the events of summer 1863, focusing on the Battle of Gettysburg and its impact on Atlanta. It describes the initial optimism of the South, the anxiety during the battle, and the aftermath as casualty lists arrive. The chapter highlights the personal losses experienced by various characters, including the death of the Tarleton boys and Darcy Meade. It also explores the emotional reactions of key characters like Scarlett, Melanie, and others to the news from the front.
scenes.scenario: The scene unfolds in the sweltering heat of an Atlanta summer day in 1863, outside the bustling newspaper office. The atmosphere is tense, heavy with the anticipation of dire news as townsfolk gather, their faces etched with anxiety and fear. These people, once brimming with confidence in their cause, now stand silent and hopeful, praying for the survival of loved ones whose fates depend on the papers inside. Whispers of recent battles and casualties ripple through the crowd as they await the news of the Battle of Gettysburg, a pivotal moment that might seal their fate. The air feels thick, almost suffocating, reflecting the internal turmoil of those gathered.
scenes.topic: Arrival of casualty lists from the Battle of Gettysburg

key_characters.name: Scarlett O'Hara
key_characters.thought: The dread gnaws at me like a persistent shadow. Ashley must be safe—he simply has to be. Yet, beneath this, I can feel Melanie's pain, her longing for what I have. I’m torn between the relief I desire and the friendship I cherish.

key_characters.name: Melanie Hamilton
key_characters.thought: My heart aches with each moment of this unbearable wait. Ashamed of the jealousy I feel towards Scarlett, I must suppress my fears. My place is to support those around me, to be their pillar of strength while I silently pray for Ashley's safety.

key_characters.name: Rhett Butler
key_characters.thought: This is a tragic play of human folly; the aftermath of blind idealism. I tread the line between cynicism and sympathy, pondering both the futility and humanity embedded in their desperation. Perhaps this news will finally open their eyes to reality.

dialogues.message: The crowd outside the newspaper office grows larger and more anxious. The air is thick with tension and the summer heat.
[My heart is pounding so hard I can barely breathe. I must know about Ashley.] Melly, do you see anything yet?
[I'm terrified, but I must stay calm for Scarlett and Aunt Pitty.] Not yet, Scarlett. We must be patient. (She squeezes Scarlett's hand reassuringly)
[These women are on the verge of hysteria. Perhaps I can offer some assistance.] (approaches the carriage) Ladies, I've just come from headquarters. The first casualty lists are arriving.
[Oh, thank goodness for Captain Butler's kindness!] Oh, Captain Butler, how kind of you to come and tell us! When will they be posted?
[Her gratitude is touching, if misplaced.] They should be out any minute, Madam. The reports have been in the offices for half an hour now.
